newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG capital hit by looting as crisis spreads.
newsitem.headline: PNG capital hit by looting as crisis spreads.

text.p: The capital of Papua New Guinea was hit by looting on Thursday as local criminal gangs took advantage of a political crisis that has seen the army challenge Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.
Police fired tear gas to stop looting raids around the city and rifle shots rang out near an army barracks that has become the focus for anti-government dissent.
The crisis, sparked by a row over the hiring of foreign mercenaries to quell an island rebellion, claimed its first victim when a supermarket guard used a machete to cut off a looter's hand.

But after a day of protest on Wednesday, Thursday's unrest appeared to be more criminal than political. In the grip of local gangs known as "rascals", Port Moresby is always one of the world's most dangerous cities.
"It's just looting," said one police officer at the scene. "People are taking advantage of the situation."

The wider political crisis continued. Senior army officers gave a defence ministry official a petition with 4,700 signatures -- representing virtually all army personnel -- demanding that sacked commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok be reinstated.

Singirok sparked the unrest on Monday when he demanded that Chan and two other senior minister resign over their decision to use foreign mercenaries to end a nine-year rebellion on the resource-rich island of Bougainville.

The petition, which set a deadline of four p.m. (0600 GMT), demanded that all those connected with the mercenary operation stand down and an independent inquiry be set up to investigate the US$28 million contract with British military company Sandline International.
"Everybody down the ranks ... are all in support of the general," an army captain told reporters at the barracks.
But he said soldiers did not intend joining in any street protests, adding: "That would defeat the whole purpose."
Prime Minister Chan signalled a climbdown over the mercenaries on Wednesday, announcing that his cabinet would reconsider their use.
The first six of 40 mercenaries, who are mostly South African, left the South Pacific nation on Wednesday and told reporters at Singapore airport that the contract had already been terminated.
Chan and his cabinet met in emergency session on Thursday morning and the prime minister also met three senior Australian officials sent by Prime Minister John Howard.

Howard has condemned any use of mercenaries on Bougainville and held secret talks with Chan 10 days ago to propose alternatives thought to involve more extensive Australian training for the PNG Defence Force. Increased Australian aid could prove Chan's best hope of ending the crisis.
About 2,000 protesters were gathered outside the Port Moresby barracks on Thursday morning and police had to fire tear gas to protect a nearby supermarket.

"A security guard inside a building grabbed a hand as it came through and chopped it off," a policeman said after the raid. The severed hand was left on a footpath while the looter ran off with his bloodied arm wrapped in a T-shirt.
The looters have targeted Chinese shops, reflecting popular resentment against ethnic Chinese businessmen. Chan himself is part-Chinese.
Although it has kept up the pressure on Chan, the army has not joined in any of the street protests.

A senior Singirok aide, Colonel Jack Tuat, was applauded by a crowd of soldiers inside the barracks on Thursday when he told them: "I know you are concerned about the happenings outside, but do not take part...All units, we must appear now at this point of time to be loyal."
